items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Communication using words, including the content, clarity and use of jargon”?
items.answer: Verbal communication
items.markingKey: Verbal communication: communication using words, including the content, clarity and use of jargon. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the use of medical jargon can harm the patient–practitioner relationship.
items.answer: Patients may not understand their diagnosis or treatment instructions, feel confused or intimidated and be less likely to ask questions or follow advice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark misunderstanding; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Explain one way non-verbal communication can improve consultations.
items.answer: Eye contact, nodding and open posture show interest and empathy, building rapport so patients disclose more and are more satisfied.
items.markingKey: 1 mark behaviour; 1 mark effect [2]

items.stem: A young doctor in Istanbul, Arjun, often wears casual clothes, rarely looks up from the computer and uses many technical terms. Older patients complain that they do not trust Arjun. Identify two features of Arjun’s communication that may reduce trust.
items.answer: Casual dress; little eye contact (looking at the computer); use of medical jargon.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A young doctor in Accra, Mei, often wears casual clothes, rarely looks up from the computer and uses many technical terms. Older patients complain that they do not trust Mei. (a) Identify two features of Mei’s communication that may reduce trust. (b) Use research to explain why older patients in particular may dislike Mei’s dress.
items.answer: (a) Casual dress; little eye contact (looking at the computer); use of medical jargon. (b) McKinstry and Wang found that older patients especially preferred formal dress and had more confidence in formally dressed doctors.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark finding; 1 mark older patients [2]

items.stem: Evaluate McKinstry and Wang’s (1991) study of doctors’ dress in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It suggests doctors could adapt their dress to patients’ expectations to increase confidence. Strength (sample): A large number of patients from several practices took part, so the results are more representative. Weakness (ecological validity): Patients rated photographs rather than meeting real doctors, so real reactions may differ. Weakness (generalisability): Expectations of dress are cultural and change over time, so findings from Scotland in 1991 may not apply today or elsewhere. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a doctor-centred and a patient-centred consultation style.
items.answer: In a doctor-centred style the doctor asks closed questions, focuses on the physical problem and makes decisions; in a patient-centred style the doctor uses open questions, listens to the patient’s concerns and shares decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why doctors may make more type I than type II errors.
items.answer: Missing a serious illness (type II) could harm the patient and lead to blame, so doctors cautiously treat or investigate when unsure, even if the person is healthy.

items.stem: Lucas, from Colombo, noticed a lump three months ago but has only just visited a doctor. Lucas says: “At first I thought it was nothing, then I meant to book an appointment but kept putting it off.” Identify the stages of delay in Lucas’s account using Safer et al.’s model.
items.answer: Appraisal delay (“thought it was nothing”) and utilisation delay (meant to book but put it off).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.answer: (a) Appraisal: no pain, so the symptom seemed unimportant. Utilisation: fear of a serious diagnosis or practical problems such as work. (b) Public campaigns about warning signs and easier, faster appointment systems.

items.stem: Evaluate Savage and Armstrong’s (1990) study of consultation styles, including a discussion of random allocation.
items.answer: Strength (random allocation): Patients were randomly allocated to directing or sharing consultations, so differences in satisfaction are likely to be due to style. Strength (ecological validity): It used real consultations in a real general practice. Weakness (generalisability): It took place in one practice with one doctor, so results may not apply to other doctors or patient groups. Weakness (ethics): Patients were not told their consultation style was being varied, although all received appropriate care. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Evaluate Robinson and West’s (1992) study of disclosure to computers, including a discussion of ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (ecological validity): Real patients attending a real clinic answered questions about their own health. Strength (usefulness): Clinics can use computer questionnaires before consultations to collect sensitive information. Weakness (generalisability): Sexual health is especially embarrassing, so patients with other conditions may not disclose more to computers. Weakness (validity): More disclosure on a computer does not prove the information is more accurate. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Looking at a computer screen for most of a consultation can reduce rapport.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “A doctor’s clothing has no effect on how patients feel about the consultation.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Patients may feel the doctor is not listening. (b) Not correct. McKinstry and Wang found dress affected patients’ confidence and willingness to see a doctor.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: McKinstry and Wang’s (1991) study of doctors’ dress can be evaluated in terms of generalisability. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Expectations of dress are cultural and change over time, so findings from Scotland in 1991 may not apply today or elsewhere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to generalisability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A young doctor in Madrid, Mateo, often wears casual clothes, rarely looks up from the computer and uses many technical terms. Older patients complain that they do not trust Mateo. Suggest two changes Mateo could make and explain their benefits.
items.answer: Wear more formal clothing and use plain language with good eye contact, building rapport and understanding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each change with benefit [2]

items.stem: Ravi compared patient satisfaction scores (1–25) after directing-style and sharing-style consultations in Auckland. Table: Satisfaction score (1–25) — Directing style: 17, 19, 20, 18, 16, 20, 16, 17. Sharing style: 16, 16, 14, 15, 16, 14, 12, 17. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Directing style: 17.9; sharing style: 15.0.
items.markingKey: Directing style: 143 ÷ 8 = 17.9; sharing style: 120 ÷ 8 = 15.0. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: A young doctor in Santiago, Mei, often wears casual clothes, rarely looks up from the computer and uses many technical terms. Older patients complain that they do not trust Mei. (a) Use research to explain why older patients in particular may dislike Mei’s dress. (b) Suggest two changes Mei could make and explain their benefits.
items.answer: (a) McKinstry and Wang found that older patients especially preferred formal dress and had more confidence in formally dressed doctors. (b) Wear more formal clothing and use plain language with good eye contact, building rapport and understanding.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark finding; 1 mark older patients [2] (b) 1 mark each change with benefit [2]

items.stem: Aisha wants to find out whether patients disclose more sensitive information on a computer form than to a nurse. Design a field experiment to investigate this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, controls, how the dependent variable will be measured and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: computer form or nurse interview; DV: number of sensitive items disclosed. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Riyadh, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Failing to diagnose an illness in a person who is ill (a false negative)”?
items.answer: Type II error
items.markingKey: Type II error: failing to diagnose an illness in a person who is ill (a false negative). [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe Safer et al.’s three stages of delay in seeking treatment. (b) A student writes: “Munchausen syndrome involves people who genuinely believe they are ill.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Appraisal delay (time to decide a symptom means illness), illness delay (time to decide to seek care) and utilisation delay (time from deciding to actually attending). (b) Not correct. That describes illness anxiety; in Munchausen syndrome symptoms are deliberately faked or induced.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each stage [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength of Savage and Armstrong’s (1990) study of consultation styles that relates to random allocation.
items.answer: Patients were randomly allocated to directing or sharing consultations, so differences in satisfaction are likely to be due to style.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to random allocation; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Jonas, from Accra, noticed a lump three months ago but has only just visited a doctor. Jonas says: “At first I thought it was nothing, then I meant to book an appointment but kept putting it off.” Identify the stages of delay in Jonas’s account using Safer et al.’s model.
items.answer: Appraisal delay (“thought it was nothing”) and utilisation delay (meant to book but put it off).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Jonas compared patient satisfaction scores (1–25) after directing-style and sharing-style consultations in Lima. Table: Satisfaction score (1–25) — Directing style: 22, 22, 17, 18, 18, 16, 19. Sharing style: 14, 17, 16, 19, 16, 12, 17. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
items.answer: Patients who receive a directing-style consultation will report higher satisfaction than patients who receive a sharing-style consultation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that the way practitioners communicate is the most important factor in the patient–practitioner relationship. In your answer, you may refer to individual differences, usefulness and cultural differences.
items.answer: Arguments for: Savage and Armstrong (1990) found consultation style affected patient satisfaction. McKinstry and Wang (1991) found dress affected patients’ confidence in doctors. Non-verbal communication such as eye contact affects disclosure. Arguments against: Patient factors such as delay (Safer et al., 1979) and misuse of services also matter. Patients may disclose more to computers than to doctors (Robinson and West, 1992). Cultural expectations of doctors differ. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Felix, from Kuala Lumpur, noticed a lump three months ago but has only just visited a doctor. Felix says: “At first I thought it was nothing, then I meant to book an appointment but kept putting it off.” (a) Identify the stages of delay in Felix’s account using Safer et al.’s model. (b) Suggest one reason for each type of delay. (c) Suggest how health services could reduce such delays.
items.answer: (a) Appraisal delay (“thought it was nothing”) and utilisation delay (meant to book but put it off). (b) Appraisal: no pain, so the symptom seemed unimportant. Utilisation: fear of a serious diagnosis or practical problems such as work. (c) Public campaigns about warning signs and easier, faster appointment systems.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is meant by ‘computerised interview’?
items.answer: A set of questions answered by the patient on a computer rather than face to face.
items.markingKey: Computerised interview: a set of questions answered by the patient on a computer rather than face to face. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Robinson and West’s (1992) study of disclosure to computers can be evaluated in terms of generalisability. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Sexual health is especially embarrassing, so patients with other conditions may not disclose more to computers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to generalisability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Robinson and West’s (1992) study of disclosure to computers can be evaluated in terms of usefulness. Explain one strength of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Clinics can use computer questionnaires before consultations to collect sensitive information.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to usefulness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A health centre in Karachi randomly allocated 6 patients to consultations in a directing style and 6 to a sharing style, then measured satisfaction (1–25). Table: Satisfaction score (1–25) — Directing style: 18, 14, 25, 23, 19, 18. Sharing style: 19, 16, 13, 15, 17, 18. Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: The same doctor using both styles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: A sexual health clinic in Bogotá finds that patients often do not mention important symptoms to the nurse. The manager, Isla, wants to improve disclosure. (a) Explain why this change might increase disclosure. (b) Explain one problem with the change.
items.answer: (a) Patients feel less embarrassed and judged by a computer than by a person, so they report sensitive symptoms. (b) Some patients, such as older people, may be uncomfortable with computers, and nurses may miss non-verbal cues.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reduced embarrassment; 1 mark effect [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Muscat is interested in how doctors use non-verbal communication in consultations. Design an observation to test this. Your plan must include: behavioural categories, ethical issues and the type of observation.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: non-verbal behaviours; categories: eye contact, smiling, nodding, looking at the computer. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Muscat, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.

Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed.
